title: The First Ember
story:
James had spent sixty-five sunrises wondering how far a single footstep could take a creature who once knew only the high green vaults of the Great Canopy. He had crossed the whistling flats, marvelled at the great engine-carts of Oakhaven, climbed the dizzying height of Cloudveil Pass, and drifted down into this quiet, sun-baked southern valley where time seemed to slow down and listen. The memory of Barnaby's ticking clocks and Silas's green sea-glass felt like distant chapters from an old leather-bound volume, yet every step of the journey lived quietly beneath his paws. Today, the morning air carried the crisp, dry scent of eucalyptus and sun-baked earth as he stepped beyond the wooden threshold of the workshop and out into the winding, dust-softened lanes of Aldea San Gabriel.

Working beside Don Tadeo had become a steady, comforting rhythm, but James felt the quiet itch of curiosity pulling him toward the outer edges of the settlement where the valley fields met the wild hills. He wandered past crumbling adobe walls and sun-bleached wooden fences, pausing to watch a cluster of yellow butterflies dance above an irrigation ditch. When a sudden gust of wind rustled the dry maize stalks, James instinctively reached into his belt and touched his small compass, watching the tiny needle settle faithfully toward the south. It was a familiar little gesture, a quiet anchoring habit born from weeks of walking unknown paths alone under vast highland skies.

By midday, James reached the old stone perimeter wall where the village faded completely into the open scrubland. He found a smooth, warm flat stone beneath a towering pepper tree and carefully unrolled Barnaby's map inside its brass canister to inspect his progress far beyond Oakhaven's borders. With his charcoal stub, he added a tiny, careful mark representing his new life in the cedar shed, anchoring his presence permanently onto the parchment. He looked out over the rolling golden hills that stretched endlessly toward the horizon, feeling that strange, thrilling lightness of being entirely where he was supposed to be.

As evening began to paint the valley in shades of amber and bruised violet, James made his way back toward the center of Aldea San Gabriel. The sky above the jacaranda trees turned the color of ripe plums, and distant cooking fires began to send thin plumes of fragrant smoke into the cooling twilight. He settled onto the low stone wall outside Don Tadeo's workshop, listening to the gentle evening chatter of the village echoing down the narrow lane. Resting his chin against his knees, he whispered his quiet greeting to the gathering dusk: 'Pleased to meet you, whatever comes next.'
